chapters.title: Chapter 4: Paying Tax Through the Year

lessons.title: TDS and TCS: When Your Business Becomes the Tax Collector

body.text: Once your business pays salaries, rent, professional fees or contractor bills, the government makes you part of its collection machinery. You withhold a slice of someone else's income, deposit it under their PAN, and report it. The money was never yours, but every penalty for getting it wrong is.

children.text: Tax deducted at source is the largest single source of direct tax collection in India, and it works because businesses do the work. Your vendor gets paid less, the balance reaches the government against their PAN, and they claim credit for it when they file. Run it well and it is invisible. Run it badly and it produces disallowed expenses, interest, late fees and, in serious cases, prosecution.

Under the old Act, every kind of payment had its own section, and finance teams spoke in numbers: 194C for the contractor, 194J for the consultant, 194I for the landlord. The Income-tax Act, 2025 folded that entire series into three provisions, with tables inside them and a four-digit payment code for each row.

cells: TDS on every other payment, arranged as tables
The rest of the 194 series, including 194C, 194J, 194I, 194H, 194A and 194T

body.text: The tax department has been clear that this renumbering changed no policy. Rates and thresholds are what the Finance Act makes them, not what the rewrite did. So when your vendor's invoice says TDS under 194J, they are not wrong about the rate, only about the address.

children.text: The Payments a Normal Business Actually Makes

body.caption: Common TDS rates and thresholds for tax year 2026-27

cells: Average rate on the employee's estimated annual tax
Once taxable salary crosses the exemption limit
1% to individuals and HUFs, 2% to others
₹30,000 for a single bill, or ₹1,00,000 in the year
Purchases above ₹50 lakh from one seller in the year

body.text: Notice the two-part contractor threshold. A vendor billing you ₹25,000 a month needs no deduction on any single bill, but crosses ₹1,00,000 during the year at the fourth invoice, and TDS then applies to the whole amount paid in the year, not just the excess. This is the single most common TDS miss in small companies, and it is created by the accounts payable process, not by the tax rule.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Payment Needs Deduction?
body.question: A company makes four payments in the year. On which one is no TDS required?
options: ₹60,000 to a chartered accountant for professional services
₹28,000 as a one-off payment to a signboard contractor, with no other payments to him all year
₹1,00,000 a month as office rent to a landlord
₹45,000 as commission to a sales agent
body.explanation: The signboard contractor stays below both contractor thresholds: under ₹30,000 for the single bill and under ₹1,00,000 for the year. The professional fee of ₹60,000 crosses the ₹50,000 annual threshold and attracts 10%. Rent of ₹1,00,000 a month is above the ₹50,000 monthly threshold and attracts 10%. Commission of ₹45,000 is above ₹20,000 and attracts 2%.

body.caption: What has to happen, and by when

cells: At the time of payment or credit to the vendor's account, whichever is earlier
By the 7th of the following month, and by 30 April for deductions made in March
Generally within a month of the quarter ending, with the March quarter allowed longer
Annually, after the last quarter's return is filed
Quarterly, shortly after each return is filed

body.text: Deduct at payment or credit, whichever is earlier. That word credit is what catches year-end accruals. Booking a consultant's March invoice as an expense on 31 March creates the liability to deduct then, even though you plan to pay in April. Provisions made at year end for services already received are a standard audit finding for exactly this reason.

stats.label: Failed to deduct
stats.context: From the date the tax was deductible until it is actually deducted

stats.label: Deducted but not deposited
stats.context: From the date of deduction until deposit. Higher, because you are holding someone else's money

stats.label: Late quarterly return
stats.context: Until the return is filed, capped at the TDS amount involved

stats.label: Expense disallowed
stats.context: Of the payment itself, under section 35 [old 40], until the TDS is deposited

body.title: Try It: The Cost of a Late Deposit
body.prompt: A company deducts ₹80,000 of TDS on a professional fee in June and deposits it three months late. At 1.5% a month, what interest does it owe? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: ₹80,000 × 1.5% × 3 months is ₹3,600. Note the rate: deducting and then holding the money attracts 1.5% a month, while never deducting at all attracts 1%. The higher charge applies to the worse behaviour, because tax already withheld from a vendor belongs to the government from the moment it is deducted. A part of a month counts as a whole month.

body.title: TDS and TCS are mirror images

columns.label: TDS under sections 392 and 393
points: You withhold from the amount and pay the vendor less
Applies to salary, rent, fees, contracts, commission, interest and dividends
Most businesses meet this every month

columns.label: TCS under section 394 [old 206C]
points: You are receiving money from a buyer
You collect extra on top of the price and pay it over
Applies to scrap, timber, minerals, liquor, motor vehicles above ₹10 lakh and foreign remittances
Most service businesses never encounter it

cells: Rates are unchanged, but challans, returns and software fields now use four-digit payment codes instead of section numbers
The familiar 24Q, 26Q, 27Q and 27EQ have been replaced. Ask your filing software or consultant which forms apply before the first quarter ends
The old rule requiring a higher rate for payees who had not filed returns is gone, removing a compliance check from every vendor payment
TCS on sale of goods withdrawn
Sellers no longer collect TCS on ordinary goods sales, though TDS on purchase of goods at 0.1% continues for large buyers
Which law applies to a payment
Determined by the earlier of payment or credit. On or after 1 April 2026, the 2025 Act applies

body.title: Scenario: The Vendor Who Crept Over the Line
body.scenario: An Indore manufacturer uses a small firm for machine servicing. The firm bills ₹24,000 every month, and accounts payable clears each bill without deducting TDS, because each one is below ₹30,000. In February, the annual total reaches ₹2,64,000. The accountant spots it while preparing for the audit in July, after the year has closed.
body.prompt: What is the damage, and what should be done now?
body.modelAnswer: The single-bill test was never the only test. Contractor payments attract TDS once the yearly total crosses ₹1,00,000, which happened with the fifth invoice, and the deduction then applies to the full amount paid during the year, not only the excess. At 2%, since the payee is a firm rather than an individual, the company should have deducted about ₹5,280 on ₹2,64,000. Three consequences follow. Interest runs at 1% a month from the date each deduction was due until it is actually deducted, and at 1.5% a month from deduction until deposit. The quarterly returns already filed were wrong and will need correction, with a late fee of ₹200 a day possible for the delay in reporting. Most expensively, 30% of ₹2,64,000, which is ₹79,200, is disallowed under section 35 [old 40] when computing taxable income, costing roughly ₹19,933 of extra tax at 25.168%, until the TDS is deposited, after which the deduction returns in the year of payment. The right move is to deduct and deposit immediately with interest, revise the affected returns, and tell the vendor so they can claim the credit. The real fix is in the payables process: tag every recurring vendor with a running annual total, and make the TDS check happen at invoice entry rather than at audit time.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Deposit Deadline
body.textWithBlank: TDS deducted during a month must generally be deposited with the government by the ___ day of the following month.
body.explanation: The 7th, with one exception: tax deducted in March gets until 30 April. Missing this date is the costliest routine slip in TDS, because interest jumps to 1.5% a month once the tax has been deducted and is simply sitting in your bank account.

body.label: When the vendor has no PAN
body.context: If a payee does not furnish a valid PAN, tax is deducted at the higher of the normal rate or 20%. Collect PAN at vendor onboarding, not at payment time.

body.title: A TDS Process That Does Not Break
steps: Collect and verify PAN before a vendor is created in the accounting system, never at the first payment
Tag each vendor with its payment type and applicable rate at onboarding
Make the TDS check happen at invoice entry, with a running annual total per vendor for threshold tests
Deduct at booking, not at payment, whenever the expense is credited first
Deposit by the 7th every month, and by 30 April for March deductions
File the quarterly return on time and reconcile it to the ledger before submission
Ask vendors to confirm the credit appears against their PAN, which catches wrong PANs early
Accept lower or nil deduction certificates only after verifying them, and apply them only to the period stated

cards.definition: TDS on salary, deducted monthly at the employee's average rate for the year.
One consolidated section for TDS on all non-salary payments, arranged as tables with payment codes.
Tax collected at source, charged by the seller on top of the price for specified goods and remittances.

cards.term: Payment or credit, whichever is earlier
cards.definition: The trigger for deduction, which is why year-end provisions for services received attract TDS.
The payer who withholds the tax, and the payee whose PAN gets the credit.
A certificate a payee obtains allowing you to deduct at a reduced or nil rate for a stated period.
The record showing what has been deducted and deposited against a PAN, which vendors use to claim credit.

points: The old 194 series now sits in section 392 for salary, section 393 for other payments and section 394 [old 206C] for TCS, with rates unchanged
Common rates are 10% on professional fees and building rent, 2% on technical fees, commission and machinery rent, and 1% or 2% on contractor payments
Contractor payments have two thresholds, ₹30,000 for a single bill and ₹1,00,000 for the year, and crossing either brings the whole year's payments into deduction
Deduct at payment or credit, whichever is earlier, which pulls year-end provisions into scope
Deposit by the 7th of the following month, and by 30 April for March
Interest is 1% a month for failing to deduct and 1.5% a month for deducting without depositing, plus ₹200 a day for a late return
Thirty percent of the expense is disallowed under section 35 [old 40] until the TDS is deposited
No PAN means deduction at the higher of the normal rate or 20%

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Rates, thresholds, forms and payment codes reflect the position understood at the time of writing for tax year 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 2025, with corresponding 1961 Act sections shown in brackets. Many thresholds changed recently and forms have been renumbered, so confirm the current chart on the income tax portal or with a qualified chartered accountant before applying it.
